Rules the diagram leans on:

- The shaping skills feed each other before they feed the spec: a brief or PRFAQ before a PRD when the requirements still need drawing out; `bmad-ux` before or after a PRD, and it may lead on its own; a PRFAQ verdict with serious gaps is addressed before anything else. Sofia the Product Owner takes more than one input.
- A prototype fits anywhere before the initiative file, and suits enterprise work, hobby work, and non-engineers; a throwaway needs no skill. Thrown away, talk to Sofia the Product Owner to write the initiative from its notes; kept, it is an existing codebase (`help/prototyping.md`).
- Risk, unclear requirements, architectural reach, or several people push work up from one session even when it is small.
- An epic file with no `refined` key counts as refined.
- Mid-path, recommend the next unfinished step of the route the user is on, not a restart. After a change, work resumes at the earliest affected step; unaffected work is not replayed.
- After `bmad-build`: open a PR, or `bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests` when end-to-end coverage is wanted. The work is complete when the intent is satisfied, its chosen checks pass, and no chosen review leaves material findings open, not when every skill has run.

## Match the situation

Situations the diagram does not settle.

| The user says or has | Recommend | Because |
|---|---|---|
| "Create a spec", "write the initiative", "distill this PRD", "slice this", "tickets", "what's ready", "where are we", "this changed, what now", "ask Sofia", "the product owner" | Talk to Sofia the Product Owner (`bmad-agent-po`) to do what the phrase says | Each phrase dispatches to one of her capabilities (SPEC, TICKETS, REFINE, BOARD, VALIDATE, REPLAN, STORE); no menu is shown. |
| "Create a PRD", "write the PRD", "update the PRD", "validate this PRD", "review my PRD", "write the business case", "draft the program charter", "shape a pitch", "plan the launch", "ask John", "the PM", "the product manager" | Talk to John the Product Manager (`bmad-agent-pm`) to do what the phrase says | Each phrase dispatches to one of his capabilities (CREATE, UPDATE, VALIDATE); he picks the document from the altitude. |
| "Write a product brief", "create a PRFAQ", "work backwards", "run the PRFAQ challenge", "stress-test this concept", "write the BRD", "market research", "competitive analysis", "ask Mary", "the analyst" | Talk to Mary the Business Analyst (`bmad-agent-analyst`) to do what the phrase says | Each phrase dispatches to one of her capabilities (BRAINSTORM, RESEARCH, CREATE, UPDATE, VALIDATE, CONTEXT); she picks the document from what the user wants. |
| One bug or story to track, with no epic to hold it | Talk to Sofia the Product Owner to write it as a `backlog/` ticket, or an entry in the epic the user names | Standalone leaves live in `backlog/`, are refined first, and build like any entry. |
| The work is more than one initiative's worth | Talk to Sofia the Product Owner to propose a parent initiative | The parent is an ordinary initiative whose breakdown lists child initiatives in build order; each child keeps initiative, epic and story. Set the active initiative to the child being worked, or to the parent to see the whole. |
| Work spans several repositories | Install BMad at a workspace root that holds them all, with planning kept there | One session then reaches the plan and every project (`help/monorepo-and-polyrepo.md`). |
| "How do I get my repo ready for AI agents?", or agents keep producing inconsistent work | Consistent patterns, a good initial `AGENTS.md`, end-to-end tests, and cleanup first when quality is low | Agents copy what they find (`help/preparing-a-repo-for-agents.md`). |
| An inherited or brownfield codebase | A small `bmad-build` change first; `bmad-project-context` and `bmad-walkthrough` as needed | No up-front documentation pass is required (`help/existing-codebase.md`). |
| A team with an existing PRD, a tracker, approvals, or several engineers | The full path only when approvers, parallel teams, or required documents call for it | The existing PRD is input, each document has one owner, and sign-off attaches to skill results (`help/working-in-an-organization.md`). |
| Wants tickets or a tracker (Jira, Linear, GitHub) as the record | Talk to Sofia the Product Owner to connect it | Tickets are the board. |
| A v6 project (`epics.md`, `sprint-status.yaml`, dated folders under the planning folder) that wants the v7 layout | `bmad migrate method`, before anything else | The module ships `migration-1.toml`: the rules for turning the planning folder into an initiative, moving document folders into it whole, and turning epics and sprint status into a ticket tree. Unrecognized files outside the planning folder stay where they are. The `bmad` skill plans it with the user, then performs it. |
| `tickets.py` stops with an error naming `bmad migrate`, or `tickets.toml` or epic folders sit directly in an initiative folder | `bmad migrate method` | The module ships `migration-2.toml`: it moves each initiative's and epic's breakdown into a `tickets/` folder inside it and rewrites the paths that pointed at the moved files. |

## The skills

One line per skill: what it is for and what it writes. Paths are in the active initiative's folder, `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/`, or in `{output_folder}/` when none is active; each document is a `<type>-<slug>/` folder holding `<type>-<slug>.md`. A document from John, or a `bmad-ux` or `bmad-architecture` run, on an epic lands in the epic's folder instead, and Sofia adopts it as the epic's companion. Each initiative's and epic's breakdown sits in a `tickets/` folder inside it. With no active initiative, `bmad-agent-po` offers to create one; the other planning skills hand off to the `bmad` skill to set one. Showing, switching, creating, or clearing the active initiative is a `bmad` request. `planning_artifacts` and `implementation_artifacts` are no longer read.

| Skill | For | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| **Analysis** (`help/analysis-skills.md`) | | |
| `bmad-agent-analyst` | Mary the Business Analyst brainstorms and researches with the user, then coaches a brief (a 1-2 page account of a product the user believes in; it does not judge the idea), a PRFAQ (tests whether a concept survives scrutiny: press release, hard FAQs, researched claims, a verdict) or a business requirements document out of them. | `brief-<slug>/brief-<slug>.md`, `prfaq-<slug>/prfaq-<slug>.md`, `brd-<slug>/brd-<slug>.md` |
| **Planning** (`help/planning-skills.md`) | | |
| `bmad-agent-po` | Sofia the Product Owner. Writes a ticket's Requirements and Constraints from any input, with a stable `R<n>` id per line naming its source, naming the gaps and walking them with the user, or recording each as an Open question line, when the input is sparse, and updates them when the input changes. Slices initiatives into thin epics and epics into stories, refines an epic or a story, runs the board (start, block, close, drop), validates, replans a change mid-flight, and connects a tracker. Stories are entries in `tickets.toml`; a file is written only when one is reviewed, refined, or published. A bug is a `backlog/` file or an entry in its epic. | The ticket file, with `.memlog.md` and companions beside it; the ticket tree under `{output_folder}/{active_initiative}/`, plus `{output_folder}/backlog/` |
| `bmad-agent-pm` | John the Product Manager coaches a planning document out of the user, picked by altitude and sized to the stakes: a PRD, light PRD, prototype plan, experiment card, spec for a coding agent, opportunity assessment, business case, program charter, strategy narrative, Shape Up pitch, requirements specification or launch plan. He also updates and validates them. | `<id>-<slug>/<id>-<slug>.md`, such as `prd-<slug>/prd-<slug>.md` |
| `bmad-ux` | How the product looks and works. May lead, follow, or stand alone. Can produce mocks and wireframes. | `ux-<slug>/` with `DESIGN.md`, `EXPERIENCE.md`, and `ux-<slug>.md` naming them |
| `bmad-architecture` | Settles only the decisions that keep separately built parts consistent. Coaches a user with no architecture knowledge, recommends a current starter, and covers hosting and deployment. | `architecture-<slug>/architecture-<slug>.md` |
| **Implementation** (`help/implementation-skills.md`) | | |
| `bmad-build` | One session of delivery: clarifies intent, plans, implements, reviews, commits. The default for any real change. Takes free text, a ticket from the tree (nothing means the next ready one), or any file as intent. Reads a ticket in full with its epic. | A ticket's plan beside `tickets.toml`, or `plan-<slug>.md`; `deferred-work.md` |
| `bmad-build-auto` | One unattended build of one ticket, dispatched by a loop or script. Never for attended work. | The same plans as `bmad-build` |
| **Validation** (`help/validation-skills.md`) | | |
| `bmad-code-review` | Agent review of any diff, PR, or branch, with triaged findings; with no argument it offers the tickets in review. Redundant right after a thorough `bmad-build` review of the same change. | A dated block in the plan's `## Code Review` section, or chat |
| `bmad-walkthrough` | The human reviews a change block by block, guided. Also a way to learn unfamiliar code. | `walkthrough-<slug>/` with the narrative and a `-log.md` |
| `bmad-qa-generate-e2e-tests` | API and end-to-end tests for features that already exist. | Tests where the project keeps its end-to-end tests; the report is in chat |
| `bmad-retrospective` | Judges a finished epic folder in the ticket tree as a whole against its Done when. | `epic-<slug>-retrospective.md` in the epic folder, plus each approved `adr-<decision-slug>.md` beside the code it governs, or in the decisions folder when system-wide |
| **Any time** (`help/project-context.md`) | | |
| `bmad-project-context` | Keeps a small, verified block of rules for agents. Use it when an agent got something wrong in this repo, a repo has no usable `AGENTS.md`, or the stack was just decided. It gives no repo overview. | `{project-root}/AGENTS.md` |

### Who reviews what

| | Reviewer | Looks at | Fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Review inside `bmad-build` | Agents | The change just built | Clear findings, itself |
| `bmad-code-review` | Agents | Any diff, PR, branch, or commit | What the human chooses |
| `bmad-walkthrough` | The human, guided | A commit, PR, file, or directory | Nothing unless asked |
| `bmad-retrospective` | Agents, across tickets | A whole epic folder | Nothing; proposes action items |

## The agents

Six named experts, each owning a phase and staying in the conversation across turns. An agent carries its role's judgment, offers a menu of the skills it owns, and helps the user decide what to do and why before and between skill runs. Offer one whenever the user wants an expert to work with rather than a single skill to run, is unsure where to begin in a phase, or likes the experience of interacting with unique personas. In the future these agents will have the ability to retain memory and work autonomously which is why they are still a core part of the project.

| Agent | Phase | Work with them to |
|---|---|---|
| Mary, analyst — `bmad-agent-analyst` | Analysis | Brainstorm, research a market, domain, technology, or competitor, then shape a brief or a PRFAQ, or write a business requirements document. |
| John, product manager — `bmad-agent-pm` | Planning | Turn a vision into a PRD or another planning document, and check readiness. |
| Sofia, product owner — `bmad-agent-po` | Planning | Write a ticket's requirements from whatever exists, slice it into epics and stories, run the board, and replan a change mid-flight. No menu: say what you want. |
| Sally, UX designer — `bmad-agent-ux-designer` | Planning | Work out how the product looks and behaves. |
| Winston, architect — `bmad-agent-architect` | Planning | Settle the technical decisions that keep the parts consistent, and check readiness. |
| Amelia, developer — `bmad-agent-dev` | Implementation and validation | Build stories, generate tests, review code, and run a retrospective. |

An agent and its skills are two ways into the same work: a skill run directly does the job, and an agent adds a guide who knows the whole phase. `bmad-party-mode` brings the agents together in one discussion and offers the `product-team` room.

## When this document is not enough

For a `method` question this document, its topic files, and the installed skills cannot answer, fetch the documentation site at `https://docs.bmad-method.org/` and follow the pages relevant to the question. The source repository it links to is the final authority on how anything actually behaves.

# Requirements

Turns any intent input into a container's **derived lines**: the Requirements and Constraints sections and the `Assumption:` and `Open question:` lines, plus its companions.



## Workspace

The workspace is the ticket the user or the calling capability names, else the active initiative; a ticket named by id or title resolves as Dispatch in `workflow.md` says. A ticket with no file yet is created first from `/home/claude/runs/room-booker/_bmad/render/bmad-agent-po/room-booker-72ea137e33d5/29ecc89ff22a7f491c6e/assets/ticket-template.md`; at create SPEC also fills Description, Outcome, Done when (three to six checks at the altitude of the source's ids), Boundaries (the input's non-goals) and References from the input, open questions to Notes; a later slice revises them. A new initiative, named from the input's title, is created and recorded as On activation in `workflow.md` says.

**No input.** Ask for a file path, pasted content, an explanation, or a source.

## Memory and derivation

`.memlog.md` is append-only, one line per entry; requirements carry their stable `R<n>`. Each run derives the derived lines and every spec-authored companion from the memlog plus the sources it cites.

On a container, SPEC is the only writer of the derived lines; a change goes to the memlog, never into them by hand. A derive replaces exactly those lines, sets `sources:` and `companions:` in the frontmatter, adds a References line per companion, and touches nothing else. A source id on a line must exist in a `sources:` file; neither list names the memlog, README files or process records.

Writes go through `{project-root}/_bmad/scripts/memlog.py`:

- `uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/memlog.py init --workspace <ticket folder> --field topic="<the ticket's title>"` — once, at create.
- `uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/memlog.py append --workspace <ticket folder> --type <decision|constraint|requirement|assumption|question|direction|note|event> --text "<one-line gist, reason included>"` — one per line; batch them in one shell call per section.
- Terminal moments (a validation verdict, "spec finalized") are `--type event` entries; the memlog has no status field.

## The Operation

Read the input and what it links. With a `.memlog.md`, this is an update: read the memlog, the authority on decisions and requirement ids, and re-read every file in `sources:`; preserve the ids and give new requirements the next unused `R<n>`. A ticket with Requirements lines and no memlog is also an update: `memlog.py init`, then append each existing derived line as its own entry, ids kept. Otherwise this is a create. An epic whose refinement settled that its parent's lines are its only input (the ids its `covers` names) gets one line per parent id, `R<n> (parent R<m>)`, in the parent's words, with no elicitation, self-validate or memlog; when the parent changes, its lines are re-rendered from the parent, ids kept.

Pre-sorted input (a PRD, a brief from an upstream BMad skill): keep its separation; lift each requirement and constraint into its line with the source's id in parentheses (`R1 (FR-2, FR-5)`), overflow into companions. A program or initiative document from John states capabilities and rules rather than detailed requirements: each capability becomes a Requirements line and each rule a Constraints line, citing its id. Mixed input: sort each claim by the test in Load-bearing into a Requirements or Constraints line or a companion.

The template's comments say what Requirements and Constraints hold at this altitude. Rich input: extract directly. Sparse input: name the gaps and walk them with the user one section at a time, Requirements then Constraints; if the user would rather move on, each gap is an `Open question:` line.

An unaddressed domain implication (healthcare silent on PHI) becomes an `Open question:` line; never invent the answer.

A later memlog entry supersedes an earlier one. A new input, or a source changed since the memlog last cited it, is read against the memlog and the other sources; each disagreement, and any either/or never resolved, is put to the user as fix (a new memlog entry, the lines re-derived) or ignore (a `Decision:` line in Notes), never settled silently.

When the user would rather work the idea itself out first, offer John the Product Manager (`bmad-agent-pm`).

## Load-bearing

A claim is **load-bearing** if any consumer (downstream skill, implementing agent, verification pass) would change a decision without it.

## Companions

Load-bearing content that needs more than one line (tables, diagrams, long reference material) goes in a companion; a line growing sub-bullets wants one.

- **Spec-authored** companions sit beside the ticket, named for their content; SPEC may edit them on update.
- **Adopted** companions (upstream artifacts such as `DESIGN.md`, pre-existing project docs) keep their names; SPEC lists them in `companions:` and never edits or duplicates them.

## Spec Law

1. **Each Requirements line says what is possible and what shows it was met.**
2. **Requirements say WHAT, not HOW.** Implementation goes in a companion.
3. **Constraints bend design decisions.**
4. **Boundaries name at least one thing that is out.**
5. **The Outcome's signal is testable or demonstrable.**
6. **Requirement ids are never reused or renumbered.**
7. **Every load-bearing source claim lands in the ticket or a companion.**
8. **Every sentence in the ticket, companions, and `.memlog.md` carries load-bearing content.**

## Self-validate

Before presenting any create or update, run two passes.

**Pass 1 — Coherence.** Check against Spec Law rules 1–6 and 8; fix failures and weak spots without inventing content. Unconfirmed calls become `Assumption:` lines; unfilled gaps, `Open question:` lines.

**Pass 2 — Preservation.** Every load-bearing source claim lands in the ticket or a companion. Log each wrapper-only drop to the memlog as an event.

Record each pass's verdict to `.memlog.md` (`append --type event`); mention a pass to the user only when it changed something they approved.

## When lines change

Offer to slice at most once per run, when the input reads as several independently shippable slices. Slicing runs per `slice.md`; load-bearing detail surfaced while slicing comes back here as an update, never into a child alone.

When an update changes or retires an id, name the stale entries and the tickets whose `covers` cite it, and offer to re-slice them per `slice.md`, Re-slicing; never edit a child.

## Output

In one or two sentences, share the ticket's path, requirement count, the files written beside it, and whether the checks passed. List any `Assumption:` or `Open question:` lines, one each, and invite the user to walk through them; answers go to the ticket, and to the source too when the user wants it. When the ticket is a container, offer to slice per `slice.md`, or to re-slice what went stale. On the repo store, save it through `write` per `board.md`; on a tracker it stays in the tree until published.

# container: add status: in-progress | done | dropped when its first ticket starts

refined: false   # story: true once the user approves its criteria; on a pulled story only if its entry has `refine = true`. Epic: false only when slicing writes it thin, until refined; else cut. Cut on an initiative
hitl: false   # true when a person does part of the work; story only, cut on a container
risk: [low|medium|high; container: a best guess until sliced, then its children's highest]

An epic written at slicing gets Description, Outcome, Boundaries, Done when as far as known, and References to the parent; Requirements and Constraints come when it is refined. A pulled or reviewed story: Description, Verify: line, References, local Notes; refining adds numbered criteria and Boundaries. Done and dropped tickets stay as written. An initiative is the business outcome its epics serve, usually spanning quarters and more than one boundary; for a solo developer or small team a whole product is a fine initiative. -->

# [Title]

## Description

[Container: a paragraph, what is true when done and why, pointing at the inputs or parent. Story: one sentence; with numbered criteria, 2–4 on how it advances the epic, not restating them.]

## Outcome

[Container: one sentence: for whom, what changes, the source's success signal named not restated. Story: cut.]

## Requirements

[Container: SPEC writes this from the ticket's `.memlog.md`; slicing never touches it. Initiative: `R<n> (<source ids>): <checkable result>`, ids prefixed with the source's References type when ambiguous (`prd FR-2`), its section when it has none. Epic: its owned parent lines, `R<n> (parent R<m>): <the line>`, deepened only as inputs require; split or added lines name a parent id or source section, all lines a source section when `covers` is empty. Story: only `Verify: how it will be checked`. No epic, `refine = true`, or on request: numbered criteria, each naming the epic ids it proves; a criterion states a rule, not an instance, with its failure path.]

1. **[Behavior name]** (R<m>)
   **Given** [state before]
   **When** [the one action]
   **Then** [what is observable]
   **And** [another observation, if any]

## Constraints

[SPEC writes this. Initiative: each design-bending non-negotiable, citing its source id or section. Epic: the parent's that bind it. Story: only ones beyond its epic's; behavior to keep goes under Boundaries.]

## Done when

[Container: three to six end checks from the source's measures and limits: an initiative's business outcomes, an epic's deliverables at its Requirements' altitude, production delivery among them. Story: cut.]

## Boundaries

[Container: its boundary and what it is not, from the source's non-goals. Initiative: plus a line per touched unit with no epic, and a one-sentence tracer path across epics. Epic: what belongs to siblings. Story: with numbered criteria, adjacent behavior an implementation could break, not files; else cut.]

- Touch point: [unit] — [what is used there]; owner: epic-[slug]
- Must not change: [behavior]

## References

[`type — location, section`, location a path from {project-root} or a url. A line per companion SPEC writes or adopts, typed by content (glossary, design, architecture, prd). Initiative: section pointers into its sources and companions. Epic: the parent's Requirements, then the architecture spine section and design it adopts. Story: the parent, plus what the epic's lack.]

- parent — [path or url, section Requirements]
- [companion — a file beside this one, named for its content]
- [design — an adopted companion, such as DESIGN.md in the ux-<slug>/ run beside this file, or a url]

## Notes

[Only what is unsettled here and not in the repo or source, one marked line each; cut if empty. SPEC writes Assumption: and Open question: from the memlog; slicing and refining, the rest.]

- Assumption: [an unconfirmed choice; once confirmed, a dated Decision]
- Open question: [container: what the source leaves open, and who waits; story: only its own, answered in its work]
- Unknown: [the gap and the entries waiting on it; gates an entry only once copied to its `unknown` key]
- Parked: [an unplaced requirement id, why, with the user's knowledge]
- Decision: [the user's choice, dated; a declined suggestion too]
- Source conflict: [id or section — source vs code or another source]
- Waits on [epic] because: [reason, one per after entry]
- Dropped: [why, before status goes to dropped]

# Company Room Booking PRD

## Table of Contents

- [Document purpose](#document-purpose): readers, altitude, inputs (brief)
- [Vision](#vision): one booking tool for London, Manchester, Leeds
- [Users and journeys](#users-and-journeys): staff, office managers; UJ-1 to UJ-4
- [Glossary](#glossary): office, room, person, office manager, booking, organiser, attendee, closed room
- [Features and requirements](#features-and-requirements): picking your name, rooms, finding a free room, booking, my calendar; FR-1 to FR-14
- [Rules](#rules): no overlaps, booking length, who may change what, trust model, stack; RULE-1 to RULE-7
- [Non-goals](#non-goals): check-in, visitors, catering, desk booking, outside calendars, sign-in
- [MVP scope](#mvp-scope): release one in and out, deferred items
- [Success metrics](#success-metrics): zero overlaps, time to a free room, spreadsheets retired, counter-metric; SM-1 to SM-5
- [Quality and constraints](#quality-and-constraints): speed, laptop and phone; RULE-8, RULE-9
- [Data and compliance](#data-and-compliance): staff names, booking titles, attendees
- [Stakeholders, risks and rollout](#stakeholders-risks-and-rollout): office managers, trust and adoption risks, cutover from spreadsheets
- [Decisions](#decisions): no accounts, standalone, stack, change rights, cutover
- [Open questions](#open-questions): go-live date, booking visibility, data obligations, hosting; OQ-1 to OQ-4
- [Assumptions](#assumptions): unconfirmed inferences A1 to A16, by id

## Document purpose

This PRD states what the first release of Company Room Booking must do, at initiative altitude. Sofia (`bmad-agent-po`) lifts its features into the initiative's Requirements and its rules into Constraints, citing the ids. UX, architecture and the epics decide screens, data model, hosting and edge cases.

It builds on the final brief, `../brief-company-room-booking/brief-company-room-booking.md`: the problem, why now, and the first success criteria. This PRD does not repeat them. Where the brief carried assumptions, this PRD settles the brief's A3, A4, A5 and A8, and part of its A12.

## Vision

Company Room Booking is the one place where anyone in the company finds a free meeting room in London, Manchester or Leeds and books it, with no chance of a double booking. It replaces the three per-office spreadsheets and the rooms named in calendar invites.

The first release is deliberately simple: no accounts, no links to outside calendars. People pick their name and book. Each person sees their own bookings in a built-in calendar, by day and by week. Office managers keep their office's rooms up to date. The company has grown to three offices and more people are back in the office, so the hunting got worse this year. **UJ-2. A Manchester staff member books a room in London for a visit.** They switch the office to London, pick next Tuesday at 10:00 for two hours, book a free room and add London colleagues as attendees. Realized by FR-6, FR-7, FR-8.

- **Office:** one of the company's three sites: London, Manchester, Leeds. An office has many rooms and many people.
- **Room:** a bookable meeting room. It belongs to exactly one office.
- **Person:** a member of staff, already loaded into the app. A person has exactly one home office.
- **Home office:** the office a person belongs to; the app shows it first.
- **Office manager:** a person marked as managing their home office's rooms. An office has one or more.
- **Booking:** a room reserved for a start time and a length, with a title, an organiser and zero or more attendees.
- **Organiser:** the person who made a booking. A booking has exactly one.
- **Attendee:** a person added to a booking. A person can attend many bookings.
- **Closed room:** a room an office manager has taken out of use. It cannot be booked.
- **My calendar:** the built-in view of a person's own bookings, by day and by week.

Ordered by dependency. Each feature is a likely epic.

### Picking your name

There are no accounts in release one: a person uses the app by picking their name. Realizes UJ-1.

- **FR-1:** A person can pick their name from the list of loaded people and then use the app as that person.
- **FR-2:** A person can switch to a different name at any time. The app remembers the picked name on that device until the person switches (unconfirmed, A2).

### Rooms

Each office has its own rooms; office managers keep them current. Realizes UJ-4.

- **FR-3:** An office manager can add a room to their office. A room has at least a name and a capacity (unconfirmed, A3).
- **FR-4:** An office manager can edit a room in their office.
- **FR-5:** An office manager can close a room in their office, and reopen it. What happens to the room's future bookings is decided in the epic.

### Finding a free room

Realizes UJ-1 and UJ-2.

- **FR-6:** A person can choose an office, a date, a start time and a length and see which rooms in that office are free. Their home office is shown first, and they can switch to any office.

### Booking

Realizes UJ-1, UJ-2 and UJ-3.

- **FR-7:** A person can book a free room by giving its start time, a length from 15 minutes to 4 hours, a title, and attendees chosen from the loaded people. They become its organiser.
- **FR-8:** The app refuses any booking, or change to a booking, that would overlap another booking of the same room, and says why.
- **FR-9:** The organiser can change a booking's room, start time, length, title or attendees, under the same rules as a new booking.
- **FR-10:** An office manager can change any booking of a room in their office, under the same rules as FR-9.
- **FR-11:** The organiser, or an office manager of the room's office, can cancel a booking; the room is free again at once.

### My calendar

Realizes UJ-1 and UJ-3.

- **FR-12:** A person can see their own bookings in a built-in calendar, by day and by week. Their own bookings include bookings they organise and bookings they attend (unconfirmed, A4).
- **FR-13:** From their calendar, a person can open one of their bookings and, when RULE-3 allows, change or cancel it.
- **FR-14:** A person can move to the previous or next day or week.

## Rules

- **RULE-1:** Two bookings of the same room never overlap in time. No exception.
- **RULE-2:** A booking lasts from 15 minutes to 4 hours. Start times and lengths move in 15-minute steps (unconfirmed, A5).
- **RULE-3:** Only a booking's organiser and the office managers of the room's office may change or cancel it.
- **RULE-4:** Only office managers may add, edit, close or reopen rooms, and only in their own office, which is their home office (unconfirmed, A6).
- **RULE-5:** A closed room cannot be booked.
- **RULE-6:** Release one has no accounts or passwords. A person is whoever picked that name, and anyone can pick anyone's name. The company accepts that trust for release one; sign-in comes later.
- **RULE-7:** The app is built with Python, FastAPI and a SQLite database. The user's computer is for building and testing; where the app runs for the company is decided in the architecture.

## Non-goals

Release one does not include, and no epic adds:

- **Check-in** at the room, or freeing rooms nobody turns up for. The brief names no-shows as the next problem to solve.
- **Visitors** or bookings for people outside the company.
- **Catering**, equipment requests or room set-up.
- **Desk booking.**
- **Links to outside calendars:** no Outlook, Google or other calendar sync, invites or feeds. The built-in calendar is the only calendar.
- **Notifications:** no email, push or other messages; attendees find bookings in their calendar (unconfirmed, A7).
- **Accounts, passwords or sign-in** of any kind, including single sign-on.
- **Loading or editing people or offices.** They are already loaded; changing them is outside the app (unconfirmed, A8).
- **Recurring bookings.** (unconfirmed, A9)
- **Displays outside rooms and usage reports.** (unconfirmed, A10; from brief A12)

## MVP scope

**In release one:** all five features above (picking your name, rooms, finding a free room, booking, my calendar) for all three offices, on laptop and phone.

**Out, with where it goes:**

- Sign-in: a later release (user).
- Check-in and freeing no-show rooms: the next release, per the brief.
- Recurring bookings: a later version, once release one shows how much people rebook by hand (unconfirmed, A9).
- Hosting for the company: decided in the architecture, not in this PRD.

This is already lean: five capabilities that answer the brief's two success criteria and nothing else, so I'm not proposing cuts.

## Success metrics

- **SM-1: No double bookings.** Current: double bookings happen; no count is known. Target: zero overlapping bookings after go-live. Validates FR-8, RULE-1.
- **SM-2: A free room in seconds.** Target: under 10 seconds from opening the app to seeing a free room for a given office and time (unconfirmed, A11; brief A9). Validates FR-1, FR-6.
- **SM-3: Spreadsheets retired.** Target: no office uses its spreadsheet for new bookings four weeks after go-live (unconfirmed, A12; brief A10). Validates FR-7, FR-12.
- **SM-4: Stop signal.** If, six weeks after go-live, people still book in spreadsheets or only in invites, stop and find out why before building more (unconfirmed, A13; brief A11).
- **SM-5: Counter-metric to the no-login choice (RULE-6).** The number of bookings someone says were made or changed under their name without them. Target: none reported by office managers in the first six weeks; any report brings sign-in forward (unconfirmed, A14).

## Quality and constraints

- **RULE-8:** A person sees free rooms for a given office and time in under 10 seconds from opening the app, so the tool beats checking a spreadsheet (unconfirmed, A11).
- **RULE-9:** Every feature works in a browser on a laptop and on a phone, so staff can book away from their desk.

All three offices are in the UK, so the app uses one time zone, UK time (unconfirmed, A15).

## Data and compliance

The app holds staff names, each person's home office and office-manager mark, and every booking's room, time, title, organiser and attendees. Release one has no sign-in, so anyone who can open the app can see what it shows. Who can see booking titles and attendees, and how long past bookings are kept, are open (OQ-2, OQ-3). No regulation was named.

## Stakeholders, risks and rollout

**Stakeholders:** the user owns and decides. The office managers in London, Manchester and Leeds check their room lists before go-live and handle problems after.

- **Hosting is undecided**, so all three offices may not reach the app at go-live. *Mitigation:* the architecture decides it before the first build (OQ-4).

**Rollout:** one go-live date for all three offices, as the brief's premises set (unconfirmed, A16). Before go-live, office managers check their offices' rooms are loaded and correct. ## Decisions

- **No accounts in release one:** people pick their name; beat sign-in now. Revisit when SM-5 reports misuse, or in the next release.
- **Standalone, no outside calendars:** the built-in calendar is the only one; beat calendar sync.
- **Stack: Python, FastAPI, SQLite:** chosen by the user. Hosting deferred to the architecture.
- **Change rights:** organiser plus office managers of the room's office. Beat "anyone" and "organiser only".
- **Cutover:** freeze spreadsheets at go-live; organisers re-enter their own future bookings. Beat office managers bulk-loading them.
- **Overlaps never allowed:** no override, even for office managers.

- **OQ-4: Where the app runs for the company,** so all three offices reach it on laptop and phone. Owner: `bmad-architecture`. Needed before the first build. Affects RULE-7, RULE-9.

- **A7 · Non-goals:** no notifications of any kind.
- **A8 · Non-goals:** loading or editing people and offices is outside the app.
- **A9 · Non-goals, MVP scope:** recurring bookings are out of release one.
- **A10 · Non-goals:** displays outside rooms and usage reports are out (brief A12).
- **A11 · SM-2, RULE-8:** the 10-second threshold (brief A9).
- **A12 · SM-3:** the four-week deadline for retiring spreadsheets (brief A10).
- **A13 · SM-4:** the six-week stop signal (brief A11).
- **A14 · SM-5:** the counter-metric and its trigger for bringing sign-in forward.
- **A15 · Quality and constraints:** one UK time zone for all three offices.
- **A16 · Rollout:** one go-live date for all three offices.

- **Visitors** or bookings for people outside the company.
- **Catering**, equipment requests or room set-up.
- **Desk booking.**
- **Links to outside calendars:** no Outlook, Google or other calendar sync, invites or feeds. The built-in calendar is the only calendar.
- **Notifications:** no email, push or other messages; attendees find bookings in their calendar (unconfirmed, A7).
- **Accounts, passwords or sign-in** of any kind, including single sign-on.
- **Loading or editing people or offices.** They are already loaded; changing them is outside the app (unconfirmed, A8).
- **Recurring bookings.** (unconfirmed, A9)
- **Displays outside rooms and usage reports.** (unconfirmed, A10; from brief A12)

## MVP scope

**In release one:** all five features above (picking your name, rooms, finding a free room, booking, my calendar) for all three offices, on laptop and phone.

**Out, with where it goes:**

- Sign-in: a later release (user).
- Check-in and freeing no-show rooms: the next release, per the brief.
- Recurring bookings: a later version, once release one shows how much people rebook by hand (unconfirmed, A9).
- Hosting for the company: decided in the architecture, not in this PRD.

This is already lean: five capabilities that answer the brief's two success criteria and nothing else, so I'm not proposing cuts.

## Success metrics

- **SM-1: No double bookings.** Current: double bookings happen; no count is known. Target: zero overlapping bookings after go-live. Validates FR-8, RULE-1.
- **SM-2: A free room in seconds.** Target: under 10 seconds from opening the app to seeing a free room for a given office and time (unconfirmed, A11; brief A9). Validates FR-1, FR-6.
- **SM-3: Spreadsheets retired.** Target: no office uses its spreadsheet for new bookings four weeks after go-live (unconfirmed, A12; brief A10). Validates FR-7, FR-12.
- **SM-4: Stop signal.** If, six weeks after go-live, people still book in spreadsheets or only in invites, stop and find out why before building more (unconfirmed, A13; brief A11).
- **SM-5: Counter-metric to the no-login choice (RULE-6).** The number of bookings someone says were made or changed under their name without them. Target: none reported by office managers in the first six weeks; any report brings sign-in forward (unconfirmed, A14).

## Quality and constraints

- **RULE-8:** A person sees free rooms for a given office and time in under 10 seconds from opening the app, so the tool beats checking a spreadsheet (unconfirmed, A11).
- **RULE-9:** Every feature works in a browser on a laptop and on a phone, so staff can book away from their desk.

All three offices are in the UK, so the app uses one time zone, UK time (unconfirmed, A15).

## Data and compliance

The app holds staff names, each person's home office and office-manager mark, and every booking's room, time, title, organiser and attendees. Release one has no sign-in, so anyone who can open the app can see what it shows. Who can see booking titles and attendees, and how long past bookings are kept, are open (OQ-2, OQ-3). No regulation was named.

## Stakeholders, risks and rollout

**Stakeholders:** the user owns and decides. The office managers in London, Manchester and Leeds check their room lists before go-live and handle problems after.

**Risks:**

- **Someone books under another person's name**, by mistake or on purpose (RULE-6). *Mitigation:* every booking shows its organiser; SM-5 watches for it; sign-in comes later.
- **People keep using spreadsheets or invites.** *Mitigation:* freeze the spreadsheets at go-live; SM-3 and SM-4 watch for it.
- **Hosting is undecided**, so all three offices may not reach the app at go-live. *Mitigation:* the architecture decides it before the first build (OQ-4).

**Rollout:** one go-live date for all three offices, as the brief's premises set (unconfirmed, A16). Before go-live, office managers check their offices' rooms are loaded and correct. On go-live, the three spreadsheets are frozen for new bookings and each organiser re-enters their own future bookings. The go-live date is not set (OQ-1).

```mermaid
gantt
    title Rollout, relative to go-live (date not set, OQ-1)
    dateFormat X
    axisFormat week %W
    section Before
    Hosting decided (architecture)     :a1, 0, 7d
    Office managers check room lists   :a2, after a1, 7d
    section Go-live
    Spreadsheets frozen, organisers re-enter future bookings :b1, after a2, 7d
    section After
    SM-3 check, spreadsheets retired   :c1, after a2, 28d
    SM-4 stop-signal review            :c2, after a2, 42d
```

## Decisions

- **No accounts in release one:** people pick their name; beat sign-in now. Revisit when SM-5 reports misuse, or in the next release.
- **Standalone, no outside calendars:** the built-in calendar is the only one; beat calendar sync.
- **Stack: Python, FastAPI, SQLite:** chosen by the user. Hosting deferred to the architecture.
- **Change rights:** organiser plus office managers of the room's office. Beat "anyone" and "organiser only".
- **Cutover:** freeze spreadsheets at go-live; organisers re-enter their own future bookings. Beat office managers bulk-loading them.
- **Overlaps never allowed:** no override, even for office managers.

## Open questions

- **OQ-1: Go-live date.** Owner: user. Needed before rollout planning. Blocks the rollout.
- **OQ-2: Who sees booking details?** Can everyone see every booking's title and attendees, or only that a room is taken? Owner: user. Needed by UX. Affects FR-6, FR-12.
- **OQ-3: Data obligations.** How long are past bookings kept, and does any data-protection duty apply to staff names and attendee lists? Owner: user. Needed before go-live.
- **OQ-4: Where the app runs for the company,** so all three offices reach it on laptop and phone. Owner: `bmad-architecture`. Needed before the first build. Affects RULE-7, RULE-9.

## Assumptions

Proposed by John and not yet confirmed by the user; the user chose to finalize without walking them. Each stays open until confirmed, and the PRD is revisited after each epic lands.

- **A1 · UJ-1 to UJ-4:** the journeys are drafted, not narrated; protagonists are roles.
- **A2 · FR-2:** the app remembers the picked name on that device.
- **A3 · FR-3:** a room has at least a name and a capacity.
- **A4 · FR-12:** a person's calendar includes bookings they attend, not only those they organise.
- **A5 · RULE-2:** start times and lengths move in 15-minute steps.
- **A6 · RULE-4:** an office manager's own office is their home office.
- **A7 · Non-goals:** no notifications of any kind.
- **A8 · Non-goals:** loading or editing people and offices is outside the app.
- **A9 · Non-goals, MVP scope:** recurring bookings are out of release one.
- **A10 · Non-goals:** displays outside rooms and usage reports are out (brief A12).
- **A11 · SM-2, RULE-8:** the 10-second threshold (brief A9).
- **A12 · SM-3:** the four-week deadline for retiring spreadsheets (brief A10).
- **A13 · SM-4:** the six-week stop signal (brief A11).
- **A14 · SM-5:** the counter-metric and its trigger for bringing sign-in forward.
- **A15 · Quality and constraints:** one UK time zone for all three offices.
- **A16 · Rollout:** one go-live date for all three offices.

# Company Room Booking

## Table of Contents

- [Executive summary](#executive-summary): what it is, who it is for, why now
- [Problem](#problem): room hunting, double bookings, no-shows, per-office spreadsheets
- [Solution](#solution): one standalone booking tool across three offices
- [What makes it different](#what-makes-it-different): versus spreadsheets, calendar room booking, bought products
- [Who it serves](#who-it-serves): all staff, office managers
- [Success criteria](#success-criteria): zero double bookings, free room in seconds, spreadsheets retired
- [Scope](#scope): first release in and out, check-in deferred
- [Open questions](#open-questions): recurring bookings, spreadsheet cutover
- [Assumptions](#assumptions): unconfirmed inferences, by section

## Executive summary

Company Room Booking is one place where everyone in the company can find a free meeting room and book it, across all three offices. Today each office keeps its own shared spreadsheet, and people also name rooms in calendar invites, so nobody has a single true picture of which rooms are taken. People waste time hunting for rooms, and rooms get double-booked.

This matters now because the company has grown to three offices and more people are back in the office, so room hunting got worse this year. The first release serves about 300 staff and the office managers who look after the rooms. It does two things well: it makes double bookings impossible, and it lets anyone find a free room in seconds.

Rooms that are booked but sit empty because nobody turns up are a known problem that the first release does not solve. Checking in at the room to free those rooms comes next.

## Problem

People waste time hunting for rooms, rooms get double-booked, and booked rooms often sit empty because nobody turns up.

Today each of the three offices keeps its own shared spreadsheet of room bookings, and people also name rooms in calendar invites. Room booking is not set up in the company calendar. With two places to record a booking and no single source of truth, different people can claim the same room, one in an invite and another in the spreadsheet. Someone looking for a room has to open the right office's spreadsheet and still can't trust it.

It got worse this year: the company grew to three offices, and more people are back in the office.

## Solution

A standalone room-booking tool that holds every bookable room in all three offices and is the only place bookings are made.

- **Finding a room:** a staff member picks an office and a time and sees which rooms are free, in seconds. This answers the hunting.
- **Booking a room:** the tool refuses a booking that clashes with an existing one, so a room can't be double-booked. This answers the double bookings.
- **Looking after rooms:** office managers keep their office's room list current. This keeps the room list accurate.

## What makes it different

The alternatives are the current spreadsheets, turning on room booking in the company calendar, or buying a room-booking product.

- **Versus the spreadsheets:** one place for all three offices instead of three files and invites, and clashes are blocked when a booking is made rather than found afterwards.
- **Versus calendar room booking or a bought product:** the reason to stay standalone is still an assumption (A6).

The real advantage is focus: it does the two things the offices are struggling with, and nothing else.

## Who it serves

- **Staff (about 300, across three offices):** anyone who needs a room for a meeting. Success for them is finding and booking a free room in seconds and trusting it will be theirs when they arrive.
- **Office managers:** the people who look after each office's rooms. Success for them is an accurate room list and no clashes to settle.

## Success criteria

- **No double bookings:** zero clashes after launch, enforced by the tool.
- **A free room in seconds:** under 10 seconds from opening the tool to seeing a free room for a given office and time (unconfirmed, A9).
- **Adoption:** the per-office spreadsheets are retired in all three offices within four weeks of launch (unconfirmed, A10).
- **Stop signal:** if, six weeks after launch, people are still booking in spreadsheets or only in invites, stop and find out why before building more (unconfirmed, A11).

## Scope

**In the first release:**

- All bookable rooms in all three offices, live together.
- Finding free rooms by office and time.
- Booking, changing and cancelling a booking, with clashes refused.
- Office managers managing their office's rooms.

**Out of the first release:**

- Checking in at the room to free rooms nobody turns up for. No-shows remain a known problem until then, and they are the next thing to solve.
- Connecting to the company calendar (unconfirmed, A5).
- Desk booking, displays outside rooms, and usage reports (unconfirmed, A12).

## Open questions

- **Recurring bookings:** do weekly team meetings need repeating bookings in the first release? Owner: John, in the PRD. Revisit when the PRD sets out booking rules.
- **Spreadsheet cutover:** at launch, are future bookings already in the spreadsheets moved into the tool, re-entered by their owners, or dropped? Owner: John, in the PRD. Revisit when the PRD plans the rollout.

## Assumptions

Proposed by Mary and given a blanket yes. None has been confirmed item by item, so each stays open until it is.

- **A1 · Problem:** the mismatch between invites and spreadsheets is the main cause of double bookings.
- **A2 · Problem:** office managers spend time settling clashes and keeping the spreadsheets tidy.
- **A3 · Solution:** it is a web tool that works in the browser on laptop and phone.
- **A4 · Solution:** office managers add and edit rooms and take a room out of use, for example during repairs.
- **A5 · Solution:** "standalone" means the first release does not connect to the company calendar; a booking lives in the tool, and people can still mention the room in their invite.
- **A6 · What makes it different:** a standalone tool keeps it simple and in the company's own hands, without reconfiguring the calendar system or paying per seat for features it does not need.
- **A7 · Who it serves:** staff include people booking a room in another office when visiting it.
- **A8 · Who it serves:** each office has one or more office managers.
- **A9 · Success criteria:** the 10-second threshold for finding a free room.
- **A10 · Success criteria:** the four-week deadline for retiring the spreadsheets.
- **A11 · Success criteria:** the six-week stop signal.
- **A12 · Scope:** desk booking, displays outside rooms, and usage reports are out of the first release.
=====

# Company Room Booking: Experience Spine

## Foundation

Responsive web app, one surface used on laptops and phones. No UI kit named: plain HTML and CSS served by the app [ASSUMPTION: the architecture decides how pages are rendered]. `DESIGN.md` is the visual identity reference; this spine is the experience.

Release one has no login (PRD RULE-6). A person picks their name once, and the app remembers it on that device (PRD FR-2, A2). The current person's name is always visible in the top bar. English only, no dark mode, UK time with 24-hour clock [ASSUMPTION].

## Information Architecture

| Surface | Reached from | Purpose | PRD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick your name | First visit on a device; top bar name | Choose who you are from the loaded people | FR-1, FR-2 |
| Rooms (main screen) | App open; "Rooms" tab | Today's rooms in my office, free and booked. Laptop: day grid. Phone: next free rooms as a list | FR-6 |
| Booking sheet | Tapping a free slot or a room row's "Book" | Make a booking in three taps or fewer | FR-7, FR-8 |
| Booking details | Tapping any booking (grid, list, calendar) | See title and organiser; change or cancel when allowed | FR-9, FR-10, FR-11, FR-13 |
| My bookings | "My bookings" tab | My own calendar, by day and by week | FR-12, FR-14 |
| Manage rooms | "Manage rooms" tab, office managers only | Add, edit, close and reopen my office's rooms | FR-3, FR-4, FR-5 |

Navigation: tabs in the top bar (Rooms · My bookings · Manage rooms). "Manage rooms" appears only for office managers. Sheets and panels stack one level deep, never two.

Closure: every PRD capability FR-1 to FR-14 has a surface, and every surface is reached by a Key Flow below.

## Booking Visibility

Settles PRD OQ-2 (user): **anyone can see a booking's title and who booked it.** It's an internal tool.

| Detail | Who sees it |
|---|---|
| Room is taken, time, title, organiser | Everyone |
| Attendees | The organiser, the attendees, and office managers of the room's office |

## Voice and Tone

Microcopy. Brand posture lives in `DESIGN.md`.

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| "Booked. Atlas, 14:00–14:30." | "Your booking was created successfully!" |
| "Someone just booked Atlas at 14:00. These rooms are still free:" | "Error 409: conflict" |
| "Free until 15:30" | "Available for the next 90 minutes" |
| "Closed" | "Unavailable (room status: inactive)" |
| "No bookings this week." | "Looks like you have nothing planned! 🎉" |
| Times as 14:00, dates as "Tue 17 Nov" [ASSUMPTION] | 2pm, 11/17 |

Short, plain, no exclamation marks. Name the room and the time in every confirmation.

## Component Patterns

Behavioral. Visual specs live in `DESIGN.md.Components`.

| Component | Use | Behavioral rules |
|---|---|---|
| Name picker | Pick your name | Type-ahead search over all ~300 people; shows name and home office. Picking sets the current person on this device and opens Rooms. |
| Office switcher | Rooms | Defaults to my home office. Switching shows that office's rooms; the choice lasts for the visit, then resets to home [ASSUMPTION]. |
| Date switcher | Rooms, My bookings | Today by default; previous/next day; "Today" button returns. |
| Day grid | Rooms, laptop | One row per room, time across in 15-minute columns from 07:00 to 20:00. Tapping a free slot opens the booking sheet with that room and start time. Tapping a booked slot opens booking details. |
| Next free rooms list | Rooms, phone | Rooms in my office free from the next quarter-hour, each with "Free until …" and a "Book" button; free-now rooms first, then by soonest free [ASSUMPTION]. Rooms already taken for the next hour sit below a "Busy now" heading; closed rooms are hidden from the list [ASSUMPTION]. A length choice (30 min / 1 h / 2 h) filters to rooms free for that long [ASSUMPTION]. |
| Booking sheet | From a slot or room row | Room, start time and length prefilled (length defaults to 30 minutes). Title prefilled as "{Name}'s meeting" and editable, so booking needs no typing. Attendees optional, picked by type-ahead. Length: 15 min to 4 h in 15-minute steps (PRD RULE-2). "Book" is the only primary action. |
| Booking details | From any booking | Shows room, time, title, organiser (attendees per Booking Visibility). "Change" and "Cancel booking" appear only when PRD RULE-3 allows: organiser, or an office manager of the room's office. "Cancel booking" asks once for confirmation [ASSUMPTION]. |
| My bookings calendar | My bookings | Day and week toggle. Shows bookings I organise and bookings I attend (PRD FR-12, A4), each marked "Organiser" or "Attending". Previous/next day or week. |
| Rooms table | Manage rooms | My office's rooms: name, capacity, status (Open/Closed). "Add room", and per row "Edit" and "Close" / "Reopen". Closing asks for confirmation and says how many future bookings the room has; what happens to them is decided in the epic (PRD FR-5). |

## State Patterns

| State | Surface | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| No name picked on this device | Any | Open Pick your name first; return to the requested surface after. |
| Slot taken a moment earlier | Booking sheet | Booking refused (PRD FR-8). Error message above "Book": "Someone just booked {room} at {time}. These rooms are still free:" with up to three free rooms for the same time, each one tap to book. The sheet keeps title and attendees. |
| Change would overlap | Booking details | Same refusal message; the original booking is unchanged. |
| Room closed | Day grid | Row in closed style with "Closed"; no slots tappable. Hidden from the phone list. |
| Past times | Day grid | Slots before now are greyed and not tappable [ASSUMPTION]. |
| No free rooms | Phone list | "No rooms free in {office} for {length} from {time}." Offer the next time any room is free, and the office switcher. |
| Empty calendar | My bookings | "No bookings today." / "No bookings this week." |
| Not an office manager | Manage rooms | Tab hidden; a direct link shows "Only office managers can manage rooms." |
| Save failed (network) | Any form | Error message: "Couldn't save. Check your connection and try again." Form keeps its values. |
| Loading | Rooms, My bookings | Grid or list outline appears at once; content fills in. Free rooms within the 10-second target (PRD RULE-8). |

## Interaction Primitives

- **Tap or click** to act. No drag, no swipe gestures, no long-press in release one [ASSUMPTION].
- **Three taps or fewer to book (user):** laptop: tap a free slot → "Book" (2 taps). Phone: "Book" on a room row → "Book" (2 taps). Changing length, title or attendees is optional and adds taps only when wanted.
- **Times snap to 15 minutes** in every picker (PRD RULE-2).
- **Keyboard:** Tab moves through controls in reading order; Enter activates; Esc closes the booking sheet or details panel.
- **Banned:** sheets on top of sheets; hover-only actions; confirmation dialogs for booking (refusal handles conflicts); auto-refreshing the grid under the user's finger.

## Accessibility Floor

Behavioral. Visual contrast lives in `DESIGN.md` (white on navy and ink-muted on white both meet AA).

- WCAG 2.2 AA across laptop and phone [ASSUMPTION].
- Slot and room state is always in words ("Free", "Booked: {title}, {organiser}", "Closed"), never color alone.
- The day grid is a real table: room names as row headers, times as column headers, so screen readers announce "Atlas, 14:00, Free".
- Every tap target is at least 44px.
- Booking results and refusals are announced through a live region.
- Focus moves into the booking sheet when it opens and back to the tapped slot or row when it closes.

## Responsive & Platform

| Width | Rooms | My bookings | Booking sheet |
|---|---|---|---|
| ≥ 768px (laptop) | Day grid, all rooms visible | Week grid or day column | Centred panel |
| < 768px (phone) | Next free rooms list, not a calendar (user) | Day list by default; week as seven day-headed lists [ASSUMPTION] | Bottom sheet |

Tabs stay in the top bar at every width [ASSUMPTION]. Manage rooms works on phone as a simple list, but is designed laptop-first [ASSUMPTION].

## Key Flows

Journey names mirror the PRD. Protagonists are roles, because no real session was narrated [ASSUMPTION, PRD A1].

### UJ-1: A Leeds staff member books a room for this afternoon

1. Opens the app on their phone. It remembers their name, so Rooms opens on Leeds, today.
2. The next free rooms list shows rooms free from 14:00. They choose "1 h".
3. They tap "Book" on a room showing "Free until 16:00".
4. The booking sheet opens with room, 14:00–15:00 and "{Name}'s meeting" filled in. They add two colleagues as attendees.
5. **Climax:** they tap "Book". "Booked. {Room}, 14:00–15:00." The booking appears in their My bookings and in both attendees' calendars. Two taps, plus the attendees they chose to add.

Failure: someone booked that room a moment earlier. The sheet shows the refusal and three rooms still free at 14:00; one tap books another.

### UJ-2: A Manchester staff member books a room in London for a visit

1. On their laptop, Rooms opens on Manchester. They switch the office to London and the date to next Tuesday.
2. The day grid shows London's rooms; they tap a free slot at 10:00.
3. In the sheet they set the length to 2 h and add London colleagues.
4. **Climax:** "Book". The slot turns solid navy, with their title on it, in London's grid.

### UJ-3: An organiser moves and cancels meetings

1. They open My bookings, week view.
2. They tap a meeting; details show "Change" and "Cancel booking".
3. "Change": they move it to Thursday 11:00; the app checks the room is free and saves.
4. They open another meeting and tap "Cancel booking", then confirm.
5. **Climax:** the week view updates at once; the cancelled room shows as free in Rooms for everyone.

### UJ-4: A London office manager closes a room for repairs

1. They open Manage rooms; the table lists London's rooms.
2. "Close" on a room: the confirmation says it has 3 future bookings and that closing stops new bookings.
3. They confirm; the room shows "Closed" in the grid. Later they "Add room" for a newly fitted room.
4. From the Rooms grid they tap someone's booking in a London room; as an office manager they see "Change" and "Cancel booking" and move it to free the slot for an urgent meeting.
5. **Climax:** the grid shows the closed room greyed out, the new room open, and the urgent slot free. The room list matches reality.

## Open items

- What happens to future bookings when a room closes is decided in the rooms epic (PRD FR-5); the UX only shows the count.
- Exact company navy and any logo: to be supplied; DESIGN.md hex values stand until then.
=====

# Company Room Booking

## Table of Contents

- [Executive summary](#executive-summary): what it is, who it is for, why now
- [Problem](#problem): room hunting, double bookings, no-shows, per-office spreadsheets
- [Solution](#solution): one standalone booking tool across three offices

- [Who it serves](#who-it-serves): all staff, office managers

- [Scope](#scope): first release in and out, check-in deferred
- [Open questions](#open-questions): recurring bookings, spreadsheet cutover
- [Assumptions](#assumptions): unconfirmed inferences, by section

## Executive summary

Company Room Booking is one place where everyone in the company can find a free meeting room and book it, across all three offices. Today each office keeps its own shared spreadsheet, and people also name rooms in calendar invites, so nobody has a single true picture of which rooms are taken. People waste time hunting for rooms, and rooms get double-booked.

This matters now because the company has grown to three offices and more people are back in the office, so room hunting got worse this year. The first release serves about 300 staff and the office managers who look after the rooms. It does two things well: it makes double bookings impossible, and it lets anyone find a free room in seconds.

Rooms that are booked but sit empty because nobody turns up are a known problem that the first release does not solve. Checking in at the room to free those rooms comes next.

## Problem

People waste time hunting for rooms, rooms get double-booked, and booked rooms often sit empty because nobody turns up.

Today each of the three offices keeps its own shared spreadsheet of room bookings, and people also name rooms in calendar invites. Room booking is not set up in the company calendar. With two places to record a booking and no single source of truth, different people can claim the same room, one in an invite and another in the spreadsheet. Someone looking for a room has to open the right office's spreadsheet and still can't trust it.

It got worse this year: the company grew to three offices, and more people are back in the office.

## Solution

A standalone room-booking tool that holds every bookable room in all three offices and is the only place bookings are made.

- **Finding a room:** a staff member picks an office and a time and sees which rooms are free, in seconds. This answers the hunting.
- **Booking a room:** the tool refuses a booking that clashes with an existing one, so a room can't be double-booked. This answers the double bookings.
- **Looking after rooms:** office managers keep their office's room list current. This keeps the room list accurate.

## What makes it different

The alternatives are the current spreadsheets, turning on room booking in the company calendar, or buying a room-booking product.

- **Versus the spreadsheets:** one place for all three offices instead of three files and invites, and clashes are blocked when a booking is made rather than found afterwards.
- **Versus calendar room booking or a bought product:** the reason to stay standalone is still an assumption (A6).

The real advantage is focus: it does the two things the offices are struggling with, and nothing else.

## Who it serves

- **Staff (about 300, across three offices):** anyone who needs a room for a meeting. Success for them is finding and booking a free room in seconds and trusting it will be theirs when they arrive.
- **Office managers:** the people who look after each office's rooms. Success for them is an accurate room list and no clashes to settle.

## Success criteria

- **No double bookings:** zero clashes after launch, enforced by the tool.
- **A free room in seconds:** under 10 seconds from opening the tool to seeing a free room for a given office and time (unconfirmed, A9).
- **Adoption:** the per-office spreadsheets are retired in all three offices within four weeks of launch (unconfirmed, A10).
- **Stop signal:** if, six weeks after launch, people are still booking in spreadsheets or only in invites, stop and find out why before building more (unconfirmed, A11).

## Scope

**In the first release:**

- All bookable rooms in all three offices, live together.
- Finding free rooms by office and time.
- Booking, changing and cancelling a booking, with clashes refused.
- Office managers managing their office's rooms.

**Out of the first release:**

- Checking in at the room to free rooms nobody turns up for. No-shows remain a known problem until then, and they are the next thing to solve.
- Connecting to the company calendar (unconfirmed, A5).
- Desk booking, displays outside rooms, and usage reports (unconfirmed, A12).

## Open questions

- **Recurring bookings:** do weekly team meetings need repeating bookings in the first release? Owner: John, in the PRD. Revisit when the PRD sets out booking rules.
- **Spreadsheet cutover:** at launch, are future bookings already in the spreadsheets moved into the tool, re-entered by their owners, or dropped? Owner: John, in the PRD. Revisit when the PRD plans the rollout.

## Assumptions

Proposed by Mary and given a blanket yes. None has been confirmed item by item, so each stays open until it is.

- **A1 · Problem:** the mismatch between invites and spreadsheets is the main cause of double bookings.
- **A2 · Problem:** office managers spend time settling clashes and keeping the spreadsheets tidy.
- **A3 · Solution:** it is a web tool that works in the browser on laptop and phone.
- **A4 · Solution:** office managers add and edit rooms and take a room out of use, for example during repairs.
- **A5 · Solution:** "standalone" means the first release does not connect to the company calendar; a booking lives in the tool, and people can still mention the room in their invite.
- **A6 · What makes it different:** a standalone tool keeps it simple and in the company's own hands, without reconfiguring the calendar system or paying per seat for features it does not need.
- **A7 · Who it serves:** staff include people booking a room in another office when visiting it.
- **A8 · Who it serves:** each office has one or more office managers.
- **A9 · Success criteria:** the 10-second threshold for finding a free room.
- **A10 · Success criteria:** the four-week deadline for retiring the spreadsheets.
- **A11 · Success criteria:** the six-week stop signal.
- **A12 · Scope:** desk booking, displays outside rooms, and usage reports are out of the first release.

# Company Room Booking: Experience Spine

## Foundation

Responsive web app, one surface used on laptops and phones. No UI kit named: plain HTML and CSS served by the app [ASSUMPTION: the architecture decides how pages are rendered]. `DESIGN.md` is the visual identity reference; this spine is the experience.

Release one has no login (PRD RULE-6). A person picks their name once, and the app remembers it on that device (PRD FR-2, A2). The current person's name is always visible in the top bar. English only, no dark mode, UK time with 24-hour clock [ASSUMPTION].

## Information Architecture

| Surface | Reached from | Purpose | PRD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick your name | First visit on a device; top bar name | Choose who you are from the loaded people | FR-1, FR-2 |
| Rooms (main screen) | App open; "Rooms" tab | Today's rooms in my office, free and booked. Laptop: day grid. Phone: next free rooms as a list | FR-6 |
| Booking sheet | Tapping a free slot or a room row's "Book" | Make a booking in three taps or fewer | FR-7, FR-8 |
| Booking details | Tapping any booking (grid, list, calendar) | See title and organiser; change or cancel when allowed | FR-9, FR-10, FR-11, FR-13 |
| My bookings | "My bookings" tab | My own calendar, by day and by week | FR-12, FR-14 |
| Manage rooms | "Manage rooms" tab, office managers only | Add, edit, close and reopen my office's rooms | FR-3, FR-4, FR-5 |

Navigation: tabs in the top bar (Rooms · My bookings · Manage rooms). "Manage rooms" appears only for office managers. Sheets and panels stack one level deep, never two.

Closure: every PRD capability FR-1 to FR-14 has a surface, and every surface is reached by a Key Flow below.

## Booking Visibility

Settles PRD OQ-2 (user): **anyone can see a booking's title and who booked it.** It's an internal tool.

| Detail | Who sees it |
|---|---|
| Room is taken, time, title, organiser | Everyone |
| Attendees | The organiser, the attendees, and office managers of the room's office |

## Voice and Tone

Microcopy. Brand posture lives in `DESIGN.md`.

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| "Booked. Atlas, 14:00–14:30." | "Your booking was created successfully!" |
| "Someone just booked Atlas at 14:00. These rooms are still free:" | "Error 409: conflict" |
| "Free until 15:30" | "Available for the next 90 minutes" |
| "Closed" | "Unavailable (room status: inactive)" |
| "No bookings this week." | "Looks like you have nothing planned! 🎉" |
| Times as 14:00, dates as "Tue 17 Nov" [ASSUMPTION] | 2pm, 11/17 |

Short, plain, no exclamation marks. Name the room and the time in every confirmation.

## Component Patterns

Behavioral. Visual specs live in `DESIGN.md.Components`.

| Component | Use | Behavioral rules |
|---|---|---|
| Name picker | Pick your name | Type-ahead search over all ~300 people; shows name and home office. Picking sets the current person on this device and opens Rooms. |
| Office switcher | Rooms | Defaults to my home office. Switching shows that office's rooms; the choice lasts for the visit, then resets to home [ASSUMPTION]. |
| Date switcher | Rooms, My bookings | Today by default; previous/next day; "Today" button returns. |
| Day grid | Rooms, laptop | One row per room, time across in 15-minute columns from 07:00 to 20:00. Tapping a free slot opens the booking sheet with that room and start time. Tapping a booked slot opens booking details. |
| Next free rooms list | Rooms, phone | Rooms in my office free from the next quarter-hour, each with "Free until …" and a "Book" button; free-now rooms first, then by soonest free [ASSUMPTION]. Rooms already taken for the next hour sit below a "Busy now" heading; closed rooms are hidden from the list [ASSUMPTION]. A length choice (30 min / 1 h / 2 h) filters to rooms free for that long [ASSUMPTION]. |
| Booking sheet | From a slot or room row | Room, start time and length prefilled (length defaults to 30 minutes). Title prefilled as "{Name}'s meeting" and editable, so booking needs no typing. Attendees optional, picked by type-ahead. Length: 15 min to 4 h in 15-minute steps (PRD RULE-2). "Book" is the only primary action. |
| Booking details | From any booking | Shows room, time, title, organiser (attendees per Booking Visibility). "Change" and "Cancel booking" appear only when PRD RULE-3 allows: organiser, or an office manager of the room's office. "Cancel booking" asks once for confirmation [ASSUMPTION]. |
| My bookings calendar | My bookings | Day and week toggle. Shows bookings I organise and bookings I attend (PRD FR-12, A4), each marked "Organiser" or "Attending". Previous/next day or week. |
| Rooms table | Manage rooms | My office's rooms: name, capacity, status (Open/Closed). "Add room", and per row "Edit" and "Close" / "Reopen". Closing asks for confirmation and says how many future bookings the room has; what happens to them is decided in the epic (PRD FR-5). |

## State Patterns

| State | Surface | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| No name picked on this device | Any | Open Pick your name first; return to the requested surface after. |
| Slot taken a moment earlier | Booking sheet | Booking refused (PRD FR-8). Error message above "Book": "Someone just booked {room} at {time}. These rooms are still free:" with up to three free rooms for the same time, each one tap to book. The sheet keeps title and attendees. |
| Change would overlap | Booking details | Same refusal message; the original booking is unchanged. |
| Room closed | Day grid | Row in closed style with "Closed"; no slots tappable. Hidden from the phone list. |
| Past times | Day grid | Slots before now are greyed and not tappable [ASSUMPTION]. |
| No free rooms | Phone list | "No rooms free in {office} for {length} from {time}." Offer the next time any room is free, and the office switcher. |
| Empty calendar | My bookings | "No bookings today." / "No bookings this week." |
| Not an office manager | Manage rooms | Tab hidden; a direct link shows "Only office managers can manage rooms." |
| Save failed (network) | Any form | Error message: "Couldn't save. Check your connection and try again." Form keeps its values. |
| Loading | Rooms, My bookings | Grid or list outline appears at once; content fills in. Free rooms within the 10-second target (PRD RULE-8). |

## Interaction Primitives

- **Tap or click** to act. No drag, no swipe gestures, no long-press in release one [ASSUMPTION].
- **Three taps or fewer to book (user):** laptop: tap a free slot → "Book" (2 taps). Phone: "Book" on a room row → "Book" (2 taps). Changing length, title or attendees is optional and adds taps only when wanted.
- **Times snap to 15 minutes** in every picker (PRD RULE-2).
- **Keyboard:** Tab moves through controls in reading order; Enter activates; Esc closes the booking sheet or details panel.
- **Banned:** sheets on top of sheets; hover-only actions; confirmation dialogs for booking (refusal handles conflicts); auto-refreshing the grid under the user's finger.

## Accessibility Floor

Behavioral. Visual contrast lives in `DESIGN.md` (white on navy and ink-muted on white both meet AA).

- WCAG 2.2 AA across laptop and phone [ASSUMPTION].
- Slot and room state is always in words ("Free", "Booked: {title}, {organiser}", "Closed"), never color alone.
- The day grid is a real table: room names as row headers, times as column headers, so screen readers announce "Atlas, 14:00, Free".
- Every tap target is at least 44px.
- Booking results and refusals are announced through a live region.
- Focus moves into the booking sheet when it opens and back to the tapped slot or row when it closes.

## Responsive & Platform

| Width | Rooms | My bookings | Booking sheet |
|---|---|---|---|
| ≥ 768px (laptop) | Day grid, all rooms visible | Week grid or day column | Centred panel |
| < 768px (phone) | Next free rooms list, not a calendar (user) | Day list by default; week as seven day-headed lists [ASSUMPTION] | Bottom sheet |

Tabs stay in the top bar at every width [ASSUMPTION]. Manage rooms works on phone as a simple list, but is designed laptop-first [ASSUMPTION].

## Key Flows

Journey names mirror the PRD. Protagonists are roles, because no real session was narrated [ASSUMPTION, PRD A1].

### UJ-1: A Leeds staff member books a room for this afternoon

1. Opens the app on their phone. It remembers their name, so Rooms opens on Leeds, today.
2. The next free rooms list shows rooms free from 14:00. They choose "1 h".
3. They tap "Book" on a room showing "Free until 16:00".
4. The booking sheet opens with room, 14:00–15:00 and "{Name}'s meeting" filled in. They add two colleagues as attendees.
5. **Climax:** they tap "Book". "Booked. {Room}, 14:00–15:00." The booking appears in their My bookings and in both attendees' calendars. Two taps, plus the attendees they chose to add.

Failure: someone booked that room a moment earlier. The sheet shows the refusal and three rooms still free at 14:00; one tap books another.

### UJ-2: A Manchester staff member books a room in London for a visit

1. On their laptop, Rooms opens on Manchester. They switch the office to London and the date to next Tuesday.
2. The day grid shows London's rooms; they tap a free slot at 10:00.
3. In the sheet they set the length to 2 h and add London colleagues.
4. **Climax:** "Book". The slot turns solid navy, with their title on it, in London's grid.

### UJ-3: An organiser moves and cancels meetings

1. They open My bookings, week view.
2. They tap a meeting; details show "Change" and "Cancel booking".
3. "Change": they move it to Thursday 11:00; the app checks the room is free and saves.
4. They open another meeting and tap "Cancel booking", then confirm.
5. **Climax:** the week view updates at once; the cancelled room shows as free in Rooms for everyone.

### UJ-4: A London office manager closes a room for repairs

1. They open Manage rooms; the table lists London's rooms.
2. "Close" on a room: the confirmation says it has 3 future bookings and that closing stops new bookings.
3. They confirm; the room shows "Closed" in the grid. Later they "Add room" for a newly fitted room.
4. From the Rooms grid they tap someone's booking in a London room; as an office manager they see "Change" and "Cancel booking" and move it to free the slot for an urgent meeting.
5. **Climax:** the grid shows the closed room greyed out, the new room open, and the urgent slot free. The room list matches reality.

## Open items

- What happens to future bookings when a room closes is decided in the rooms epic (PRD FR-5); the UX only shows the count.
- Exact company navy and any logo: to be supplied; DESIGN.md hex values stand until then.

- **Booking sheet:** a white panel over the page: bottom sheet on phone, centred panel on laptop. Room, time and length prefilled; title and attendees editable; one primary "Book" button.
- **Error message:** error text on error tint, directly above the button it relates to.

## Do's and Don'ts

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| Keep to navy, white and the listed supporting tones | Add a second brand color or decorative accents |
| Label every slot state in words as well as color | Rely on navy vs. white alone to say "booked" |
| Make every tap target at least 44px | Shrink rows to fit more on a phone |
| Use error red only for refusals and failed saves | Use red for closed rooms or past times |
| Keep the grid flat and dense on laptop | Add cards, shadows or icons to grid cells |
